ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a transistor current gain β test circuit. On the left there is op-amp A1, a +10 V power supply connected to the relevant node through R1=3 kΩ, and also a +4 V reference connected to the input terminal of A1; the collector current of the transistor is labeled IC. On the right there is op-amp A2, feedback resistor R2=10 kΩ returns from the output terminal to the base/summing node, the output terminal u0 is connected to voltmeter V, and the figure also labels base current IB. Reasoning: According to the operating mode of the test circuit in the figure, A1 keeps the transistor collector node at +4 V, so the voltage across R1 is 10 V−4 V=6 V. The input current of an ideal op-amp is zero, so the R1 current is the collector current: IC=6 V/3 kΩ=2 mA. A2 forms an inverting current-to-voltage converter for the base current, and the base/summing node is virtual ground; the voltmeter reading is 200 mV, so the magnitude of base current IB=0.200 V/10 kΩ=20 μA. Thus β=IC/IB=2 mA/20 μA=100.

raw_record.question_text: Question: In the circuit shown in figure, which is a transistor current gain \( \beta \) test circuit, assuming \( U_{\mathrm{BE}} = 0.7 \, \mathrm{V} \), if the voltmeter reading is 200 mV, the value of \( \beta \) is ________.

method.method_draft: First identify A1 as forcing the collector node to +4 V. Therefore the current through R1 is IC = (10 V − 4 V)/3 kΩ = 2 mA, since ideal op-amp input current is zero. Then identify A2 as an inverting current-to-voltage converter for the transistor base current: the base/summing node is at virtual ground and the measured output magnitude is 200 mV, so IB = 0.200 V/10 kΩ = 20 μA. Finally compute β = IC/IB = 2 mA/20 μA = 100.
